title: Frida Kahlo's Life In Reverse | From a Final Canvas to a Coyoacan Nursery
description:
Frida Kahlo's life is told backwards in this episode, opening at the blue house in Coyoacan where she died in July 1954 and rewinding through the paintings, the marriages and the operations to her birth in the same house in 1907. The journey steps through her first solo exhibition of 1953, the teaching post she held from 1943, the divorce and remarriage with Diego Rivera, and the bus accident of 1925 that put her in bed with a mirror and a canvas. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the pictures appear in reverse order and the body behind them becomes clear. Dates, places and titles follow the documented record, and the accounts that disagree over her death are named as disputed.

scenes.narration: The blue house in Coyoacan where she spent most of her life is now a museum, with her bed, her easel and her clothes inside it. At auction in 2021 one of her self portraits brought about thirty five million dollars, a record for a Latin American artist. The house she left is full of objects that visitors come to look at.

Seventy years ago, on July 13, 1954, Frida Kahlo died at that house in Coyoacan, Mexico City, at the age of forty seven. The death certificate gave a pulmonary embolism as the cause. Some writers have suggested that she took too much of her medicine, and others have rejected that account, so the question remains disputed.

Days earlier she had gone out despite her health to join a crowd in the centre of Mexico City, protesting at the removal of a government in Guatemala. She arrived in a car and was helped to stand with the others. It was one of her last public appearances, and she had insisted on being there.

Two months before that, in the spring of 1954, she had finished her last painting, a still life of watermelons cut open on a flat ground. She wrote a short line across the fruit about life itself. Her hands were weak by then and she worked in short sessions, resting between them.

Through the early 1950s she had been in and out of hospital for operations on her spine, and she spent long weeks in bed between them. The pain was constant and the treatments did not fix the damage from the accident of 1925. She kept drawing and kept records of her weight and her temperature in a small notebook.

Two years earlier, in April 1953, she had her first solo exhibition in Mexico, at a private gallery in Mexico City. She arrived by ambulance and lay on a bed that had been set up for her inside the gallery, and the guests came to her in turn. Doctors had warned her not to attend, and she went.

Seven years earlier, in 1946, she had painted a young stag standing in a wood with arrows in its body, looking back at the viewer. The canvas came after more surgery that brought her no relief. She wrote on another picture of that year to keep her spirits up, and the two works were painted at home.

Two years before that, in 1944, she had painted herself split open to show a cracked stone column where her spine should be, with nails driven into the skin. She was wearing one of the plaster corsets that surgeons had fitted to her body. The picture takes the private damage of years and sets it out in the middle of a canvas.

In 1943 she began teaching at the national school of painting and sculpture in Mexico City. Her students met her in a studio full of light, and she took them to look at the old churches and the popular art of the markets. She was strict about drawing and generous with her time, and her classes filled quickly.

In December 1940 she married Diego Rivera for a second time, a year after their divorce. The ceremony was small and the guests were close friends. She was thirty three and he was fifty three, and the marriage was difficult from the start. Both of them painted, both of them kept separate studios, and both of them were unfaithful.

Thirteen months before that, in November 1939, their divorce had been granted in Mexico City. In the same period she painted two versions of herself sitting side by side, joined at the hands, one heart exposed. She had asked for the separation after years of his affairs, and the lawyers handled the property while she worked.

In the summer of 1939 her paintings had been shown in Paris at the invitation of the French poet who had championed them, and she did not like the company she was put in. Her work was labelled by others as strange, and she always said she painted her own life rather than any theory.

A year earlier, in November 1938, she had her first solo exhibition in New York, at a gallery run by a friend of the surrealists. Forty small works were shown and most of them sold. That same year the poet visited Mexico, saw her paintings and her house, and wrote about her with great enthusiasm.

In August 1937, at the request of her husband, the house in Coyoacan took in a political exile from the Soviet Union, together with his wife, and gave them the guest room. The arrangement lasted eighteen months. The two men later fell out badly, and the guests left the house in January 1939.

In July 1933, while they were living in the United States, she lost the child she was carrying in Detroit. She spent days in a hospital bed there and afterwards painted the scene on a small sheet with six objects linked to her body by red lines. The picture was one of the first she made about her own injuries.

Months earlier in 1933 she had been in New York while her husband painted a large wall for a company that had hired him. The commission was stopped and the design was never finished. She was unhappy in the city, missed Mexico, and wrote home about the money and the weather.

In 1932 the two of them were in Detroit, where he was painting big panels on the walls of an institute of art. She sat through the hot summers in a city she did not know, watching him work on scaffolding. The trip lasted more than a year and took her further from the country she knew.

In August 1931 she had married Diego Rivera in California, where he was already at work on murals. She was twenty four and he was forty four, and his fame was long established while hers had barely started. Her father recorded the event with his camera, and the couple were painted together the same year.

The year before that, in 1930, she had followed him to San Francisco for a commission, leaving Mexico for the first time. She was twenty three. The marriage had begun that year, and the two of them would spend much of the next four years travelling through the United States on his contracts.

By the late 1920s she had joined the Mexican Communist Party and attended its meetings in Mexico City. She read the pamphlets that members passed around and followed the arguments over land, workers and the government. Politics stayed in her work for the rest of her life, in the flags, the hands and the names that appear on her canvases.

Her painting had begun at home in the years after the accident. Her family had a canvas holder made so she could work lying down, and a mirror set above the bed, and she painted what she saw from there. Her first self portrait came in 1926, a young woman in a dark red dress looking straight out.

On September 17, 1925, the wooden bus she was riding in Mexico City collided with a streetcar. A metal handrail passed through her pelvis, and her spine and leg were broken in several places. She was eighteen years old, on her way home from school, and the injuries stayed with her for the rest of her life.

The first weeks after the accident were spent in a city hospital, where surgeons set her bones and her parents came daily. She was then taken home in a body cast and lay in her room for months. Her school friends visited and brought her books, and she asked them what she should do with her time.

Two years earlier, in 1922, she had entered the national preparatory school in Mexico City, one of only a few dozen girls admitted to it. She planned to study medicine and was quick at science and logic. She joined a small group of students who read together, played tricks, and called themselves by a shared name.

Eight years before that, in 1913, at the age of six, she had been ill with polio and spent long months indoors. One leg grew thinner than the other, and the neighbourhood children made fun of her. Her father encouraged her to swim, ride and climb to build her strength, and she recovered enough to run.

In the years around 1910 her father worked from a photographic studio in Mexico City, making portraits and pictures of buildings for the government. He had been born in Germany and had come to Mexico as a young man. She grew up among cameras, plates and printed paper, and she watched him pose his subjects carefully.

In 1910 the year of her claimed birth, a revolution began in Mexico that would run for a decade and change the country she grew up in. She later gave 1910 as her own birth date, which was not correct, so that her life would stand beside the revolution. Her real birth record gives 1907.

She was born on July 6, 1907, in the blue house at Coyoacan, on the southern edge of Mexico City, the third of four daughters. Her mother was a devout woman from a Mexican family and her father was a photographer from Germany. The house had a courtyard with plants and tiles, and it remained her home for almost all her life.
